co_turkey_tail.blurb: Turkey Tail is the steeper, harder-edged section of the Turkey Rocks, a granite cluster in the South Platte country known for crack climbing. Nearly everything here is traditional, with a handful of bolted lines and a lone aid route. The grades are spread across 5.8 to 5.12, with a good share of 5.10 and 5.11 leads, and several routes run two pitches. Standouts include Drumstick Direct and Whimsical Dreams. Expect a rack-heavy day on solid, sustained cracks rather than a quick sport session. The walls sit on a sunny exposure that can stay workable on cooler days, but the dirt road in can be rough or icy after snow.
co_turkey_tail.parking_note: Drive in from Pine Junction toward Deckers and Westcreek, then take the Cedar Mountain forest road as far as your vehicle comfortably allows. A road branching left about a mile past the old Big Turkey campground runs to a dead-end parking spot, and that is the shortest way in. Do not park or walk in from the Turkey Rock Ranch Estates neighborhood.
co_turkey_tail.approach: From the end of the road, a short trail climbs to the saddle between Turkey Rock and the Turkey Perch. Turkey Tail is the buttress off to the north (left) of the Perch, reached by crossing a talus field.

co_gilligan_s_island_2.blurb: Gilligan's Island is a compact mass of granite at the west end of Alderfer/Three Sisters Park, standing alone in an open meadow. It is a bouldering area with a few top-rope lines, and the problems run from V0 to V8 with the bulk between V1 and V5. Low-angle slabs on the south tip suit warm-ups, while the Captain wall and the walls on the west and east sides hold the harder tests. The Captain and Skipper are among the best known. Bring pads and a spotter, since a few problems are tall or have awkward landings. The meadow setting means little shade, and the island is rarely crowded.
co_gilligan_s_island_2.parking_note: Of the park's lots, use the second one along the access road, toward the park's western edge.
co_gilligan_s_island_2.approach: From the lot, walk north across the big open field on the Bluebird Meadow Trail until the rock island appears. The first boulders, including the Captain, are on the south side as you arrive.

ct_mystic_areas.blurb: A scattering of boulder sectors in and around Mystic, Groton and Ledyard, all within about a quarter hour of each other off Route 184. The rock is gneiss with a rough, gritty texture, offering edges, pockets, crimps and slopers, and some blocks are properly steep, caves and overhangs included. Many boulders are glacial erratics. Grades span the whole range from the lowest V grades up through V10 and beyond, so there is something for most levels. Coastal air keeps winter days mild and snow-free more often than inland, but access is touchy at some spots, so tread lightly, keep a low profile, and check local conditions before you go.

ga_lost_wall.blurb: Lost Wall is a sandstone cliff on Pigeon Mountain near Lafayette in northwest Georgia, tucked high enough that it is hard to spot from the valley. It is primarily a trad crag, with single-pitch routes roughly 40 to 120 feet tall. Expect fist cracks, roofs and vertical faces on mostly good rock, though less uniform than the famous Chattanooga-area walls. Grades cluster in the 5.8 to 5.10 range, and Booze and Broads, Guzzler and Laurel Lie are among the favorites. Almost everything takes gear, so bring a full rack.
ga_lost_wall.parking_note: From Lafayette, follow Chamberlain Road to Rocky Lane and drive up the mountain's switchbacks slowly. The trail pullout is at the fourth switchback.

id_shady_side.blurb: Shady Side is a short basalt wall of roughly 25 to 30 feet running along the Portneuf Greenway in Ross Park, Pocatello. It faces northeast and falls into shade by about noon in summer, which makes it the place to move once the neighboring sunny wall heats up. Almost everything is top rope on fixed anchors, with grades from 5.6 up to 5.12 and a lot of 5.9 and 5.10, so it works for beginners and for mileage. Boulder problems run along the base. The ground is shredded bark, with lawn and picnic tables nearby. It is a family-friendly spot beside a busy road.
id_shady_side.approach: The base is a few steps from the park path. Reach the anchors by scrambling up a weakness in the cliff or from the north end.

id_manning_crevice_bridge_area.blurb: Manning Crevice is a set of buttresses rising straight out of the Salmon River canyon above Riggins. The rock is fine-grained and not especially sticky, and most routes are cracks or lower-angle slabs, with a growing set of bolted lines, a few aid climbs and some bouldering. Most of it is 5.9 to 5.11, from short pitches to multi-pitch outings like Welcome to Manning Crevice and the long Graveyard Shift. Most routes face south or west, so afternoon sun makes them far hotter than the forecast suggests. Shoulder seasons and winter are the comfortable times, and a very early start helps on long routes in summer.
id_manning_crevice_bridge_area.parking_note: Take the Salmon River Road upstream from Riggins to the Manning Crevice suspension bridge. Park in the roadside pullouts nearby.

id_mid_cliffs.blurb: Mid Cliffs is a stretch of the Black Cliffs along Highway 21 east of Boise, cut into columnar basalt. About 100 feet of lower-angle columns split the crag into two main sections. Trad outnumbers sport here, and most routes sit between 5.7 and 5.10, which makes it one of the friendlier places at the Cliffs for moderate leads, with a smaller number of harder sport lines. Lightning Crack, Potato Flake and Boot Flake are well-liked crack routes. Midsummer heat can make the basalt feel greasy and punishing, so spring and fall are more pleasant.
id_mid_cliffs.parking_note: Leave the car in the paved Highway 21 pullout opposite the diversion dam. A dirt road continues upstream to a smaller lot.
id_mid_cliffs.approach: Walk upstream from the parking area until you reach a signed trail on the left that climbs to the base of the wall.

id_thinking_spot_the.blurb: The Thinking Spot is a granite formation a couple of hundred feet tall on the north side of Payette Lake near McCall, with views over water and forest. Most of the climbing is bolted sport, with some trad, a few top ropes and a boulder area. Grades run from easy up to 5.12, with the largest group in the 5.10s and a healthy number of 5.11s. RZR Parade and Oh Eight are among the favorites. Beginner-friendly routes sit alongside the harder lines, so it suits mixed groups, and guided courses and camp programs also use it. Check road and snow conditions in the shoulder seasons.
id_thinking_spot_the.parking_note: Follow Lick Creek Road, which becomes Eastside Drive, around to the north end of Payette Lake. The formation is easy to spot once you are there.
